Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance: This metric is intended to capture whether or not the organization specifically works to advance women’s careers. To report against 2X Challenge requirements, organizations must report this metric in combination with one or more of the following metrics that detail which initiatives are in place: Diverse Representation Policy (OI9485), Flexible Work Arrangements (OI7983), Sexual Harassment Policy (OI9088), Employment Benefits (OI2742), Fair Compensation Policy (OI3819), Fair Career Advancement Policy (OI4884), or Anti-Discrimination Policy (OI9331). To qualify under the 2X criteria, additional metric(s) must have specific benefits for women and must exceed compliance with local regulations and standards in the local context.
Citation: IRIS, 2021. Women's Career Advancement Initiative (OD4232). v5.2.

Definition: Indicates whether the organization has a written policy to monitor, evaluate, and ensure its workers' freedom of association.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote the relevant details of their worker freedom of association policy, including how it is enforced. See usage guidance for further information.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to capture the organization’s policy on Freedom of Association, which means allowing workers to form and join trade unions, worker associations, and worker councils or committees of their own choosing. Examples of relevant policies to footnote may include allowing workers to participate in the setting or revision of workplace rules and standards and distributing an employee handbook to all workers (written in their native language) that describes both legal requirements and the organization's policies and procedures on freedom of association.

For further guidance, organizations can refer to International Labour Organization standards (http://www.ilo.org/global/standards/subjects-covered-by-international-labour-standards/freedom-of-association/lang--en/index.htm).
Citation: IRIS, 2021. Worker Freedom of Association Policy (OI4364). v5.2.

Definition: Indicates whether the organization has policies in place to monitor, evaluate, and ensure worker safety.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote details around these policies, including the practices in place to ensure compliance. See usage guidance for further information.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to capture whether the organization has created policies in line with international norms to protect the safety of its workers. 

Worker safety entails placing and maintaining the worker in an environment adapted to the worker's physiological and psychological capabilities; preventing health-related departures caused by working conditions; promoting and maintaining the physical, mental, and social well-being of workers in all occupations; and protecting workers from health risks resulting from working conditions.

Examples of relevant policy details to footnote include: the process in place to assess safety risks, the frequency with which these risks are assessed, and the training and equipment provided to mitigate these risks.

Examples of training and equipment provided to mitigate worker safety risks include: safety training, required protective gear, testing of equipment, and posting of signs.

Organizations can refer to the SPI4 (http://cerise-spi4.squarespace.com/), specifically Essential Practice 5a5, for additional indicators related to worker safety. SPI4 is a social audit tool, developed for financial service providers, which can apply to any organization with both social and financial objectives.

This metric aligns with GRI Disclosure 403-8: Workers covered by an occupational health and safety management system.

Definition: Value of the organization's operating liquidity as of the end of the reporting period.
Calculation: = Current Assets (FP6926) - Current Liabilities (FP2269)
Usage Guidance: This metric is intended to capture the organization’s working capital position as of the end of the reporting period, also known as its operating liquidity (ability to meet additional or unexpected debts and obligations).

Definition: Ratio of the organization’s current assets compared to current liabilities as of the end of the reporting period.
Calculation: = Current Assets (FP6926) / Current Liabilities (FP2269)
Usage Guidance: This metric is intended to capture the organization’s working capital position. This ratio is commonly termed the Current Ratio or Net Working Capital.

Definition: Indicates whether the organization has policies in place to monitor, evaluate, and ensure appropriate working hours of employees, as well as a system to monitor compliance.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions made, including details around the policies and systems in place to ensure compliance. See usage guidance for further information.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to capture whether the organization has a policy in line with international norms in place to screen for appropriate working hours of employees, as well as a system to monitor compliance with that policy. Organizations may use this metric to screen for appropriate working hours at directly supported/financed enterprises or small and medium-size enterprise (SME) clients. Given complexity of measuring hours worked by employees of SME client organizations, checking for a policy in place is a good alternative. This metric is focused on employees’ working hours. For polices related to safety and working conditions of employees, refer to Worker Safety Policy (OI8001)     

Examples of relevant policy details to footnote include: the process in place to assess safety risks, the frequency with which the risks are assessed, and the training and equipment provided to mitigate these risks. 

Worker safety includes placing and maintaining the worker in an environment adapted to the worker's physiological and psychological capabilities, preventing health-related departures caused by working conditions, promoting and maintaining the physical, mental, and social well-being of workers in all occupations, and protecting workers from health risks resulting from working conditions.
Organizations can refer to the SPI4 (<http://cerise-spi4.squarespace.com/>), specifically the Essential Practice 5a5, for additional indicators related to worker safety. SPI4 is a social audit tool developed for financial service providers but applicable to any organization that has both social and financial objectives.

This metric aligns with GRI Disclosure 403-8: Workers covered by an occupational health and safety management system.

Definition: Year the organization was founded.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance: This metric is intended to capture the year the organization began operations.

Definition: Total length of coastal areas brought under official protection status or subject to formal conservation measures (such as coastal buffer zones, community-led conservation agreements, or enforcement of no-development zones) as a result of the organization’s activities.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to capture the extent of coastline that has been newly protected or newly incorporated into a larger protected coastal zone as a result of the organization’s interventions. 

Organizations should report the cumulative length of all segments of coastline protected during the reporting period. If multiple segments are protected, they should be summed and reported as a single figure. The methodology for calculating protected coastline length (e.g., based on geographic information systems (GIS) or regulatory boundaries) should be disclosed in footnotes.

Protection may include formal designations such as coastal protected areas, mangrove buffer zones, or other regulatory protections that limit harmful development or extraction. It may also include community-based conservation agreements that effectively safeguard coastal ecosystems.

This metric should be used in conjunction with relevant biodiversity or marine management indicators where applicable, such as Area of Marine Habitat Protected (PI1911) or Marine Area Directly Controlled: Total (OI7876).

If the organization contributes partially to the total protected length, this should be footnoted with an estimate of their proportional impact.

It is important to differentiate protection from other types of interventions, such as restoration or infrastructure development. Only efforts that legally or formally safeguard the coastline should be counted.
Citation: IRIS, 2025. Length of Coastline Protected (PI0510). v5.3b.

Definition: Total area of seaweed farming operations certified by a recognized third-party sustainability or environmental standard as a result of the organization’s activities.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to track the spread of sustainable aquaculture practices by measuring the area of seaweed farms that have received certification (e.g., ASC, Organic, Fair Trade, etc.) due to the organization’s direct support, facilitation, or implementation.

Unit of measurement: Hectares

Organizations should report the cumulative area of all seaweed farms certified within the reporting period. Certification must be by a verifiable and credible third-party standard that includes environmental, social, or quality criteria. Footnotes should list the certification scheme, standards met, and the duration of validity of the certification.

This metric may be particularly relevant for projects promoting sustainable blue economy initiatives, coastal livelihoods, or biodiversity-friendly aquaculture.

The metric is distinct from total seaweed farming area; it should only include areas that have been independently verified for sustainable practices. If an organization has played a partial role in certification (e.g., provided training, infrastructure, or technical assistance), this should be noted, along with the estimated proportion of contribution.

This metric should be considered alongside indicators related to marine biodiversity, water quality, or socioeconomic outcomes for coastal communities.
Citation: IRIS, 2025. Area of Seaweed Farm Certified (PI1142). v5.3b.

Definition: The number of individuals or households whose livelihood activities, income-generating pursuits, or productive assets have been supported, improved, or sustained through the organization's interventions during the reporting period. This may include support for employed or self-employed individuals, farmers, fishers, artisans, small business owners, or those involved in informal or community-based work
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.

Definition: Indicates natural and human-induced pressures faced by marine environments.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to describe the types of pressures affecting marine environments. 

According to European Environmental Agency, the types of pressures typically faced by marine environments are: 

Fishing pressure 
Maritime activities 
Seafloor damage 
Pollution 
Non-indigenous species 
Marine litter and underwater noise 
Other

Definition: Total surface area of marine habitats newly designated as Marine Protected Areas (MPAs), or new habitats added to an existing MPA network, as a result of the organization’s activities.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to describe the area of marine habitats newly designated as Marine Protected Areas (MPAs), or new habitats added to an existing MPA network, as a result of the organization’s activities. 

Unit of measurement: Hectares 
If an organization has multiple marine habitats newly brought under the protected status, the total area must be reported. This metric should be used in combination with Marine Area Directly Controlled: Total (OI7876). 

If the organization contributes partially or has been designated to be responsible for part of the total marine habitat protected, then that information should also be included in footnotes. 

It is important to distinguish restoration activities from protection in management of marine habitats and coastal areas. 

For example, if an organization is restoring a degraded coral reef, the intervention could involve coral transplantation or creating coral nurseries to rebuild reef structure. Once these activities are successfully completed, these areas would be considered restored, and you’d measure the area where those activities were implemented. 

If an organization is protecting a non-degraded coral reef from further harm without any direct intervention to rebuild it (e.g., through an MPA), then it would count as protection, not restoration.
Citation: IRIS, 2025. Area of Marine Habitat Protected (PI1911). v5.3b.

Definition: Total surface area of marine habitats that have undergone restoration activities.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to describe the total surface area of marine habitats that have successfully undergone restoration activities, including but not limited to coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, and the like. 

Examples of restoration activities include replanting mangroves, creating artificial reefs, transplanting corals, or restoring wetlands. The size of the area restored is calculated based on how much habitat has been physically re-established and is now in a state of recovery or improvement. 

Unit of measurement: Hectares 

It is important to distinguish restoration activities from protection in management of marine habitats and coastal areas. 

For example, if an organization is restoring a degraded coral reef, the intervention could involve coral transplantation or creating coral nurseries to rebuild reef structure. Once these activities are successfully completed, these areas would be considered restored, and you’d measure the area where those activities were implemented. 

If an organization is protecting a non-degraded coral reef from further harm without any direct intervention to rebuild it (e.g., through an MPA), then it would count as protection, not restoration. 
Organizations should provide information on the species and ecosystems targeted through the restoration and rehabilitation actions. The organization should also explain how these actions support species recovery. 
The thresholds should be calculated at the local level. For further guidance, please review Science Based Target Initiatives’ Ocean Draft v1 (Oct, 2024) and GRI Biodiversity Standards, 2024.
Citation: IRIS, 2025. Area of Marine Habitat Restored (PI2252). v5.3b.

Definition: Percentage of restored areas that show measurable improvements in biodiversity, ecosystem function, or resilience post-restoration (e.g., survival rate of transplanted corals or re-established seagrass coverage).
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to measure the percentage of restored areas that show measurable improvements in biodiversity, ecosystem function, or resilience after restoration efforts have taken place. 

For additional guidance, please refer to available international and local guidance for measurement and definition of restoration such as Society for Ecological Restoration (SER) standards, and IUCN Global Standard for Nature based Solutions.

Definition: Sustainable livelihood options made available to coastal communities that are primarily dependent on the ocean and coastal ecosystems.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
Marine livelihoods, as defined by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), refer to the various ways in which coastal and marine ecosystems support human well-being, through the provision of goods and services. These livelihoods are linked to the sustainable use of marine resources, such as fish, shellfish, seaweed, and other marine products, on which communities depend for food, income, cultural practices, and overall sustenance. 

For example, one analysis found that restoration projects create an average of 15 jobs for every million dollars invested.

Definition: Indicates whether the organization has undertaken biodiversity-related assessments to evaluate the biological diversity and ecosystem condition present on the coastal area and marine habitat that is directly or indirectly controlled by the organization.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric indicates whether the organization has undertaken marine biodiversity assessment activities, before the investment takes place and at the end of the reporting period. 

Marine biodiversity assessments help investors evaluate the impact of their investments, while adhering to international frameworks and guidelines that ensure responsible management of marine ecosystems. 

Organizations are recommended to follow international standards and guidelines applicable to the marine ecosystems they are operating in, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity guidelines; IUCN Red List and Regional Assessments; OSPAR indicators; BIOcean 5D Marine biodiversity assessment and prediction across spatial, temporal and human scales, a 2024 framework for marine biodiversity assessment developed by an international taskforce and published by Lenfest Ocean Program in 2024; the European Union’s Marine Strategy Framework Directive; as well as a 2024 harmonization study by the European Commission’s Joint Research Center regarding biodiversity monitoring and assessment methodologies for European marine ecosystems.

Definition: Total surface area of marine or coastal habitat lost, including both direct destruction and unrestored degradation, as a result of the financed activity, such as coastal infrastructure development, dredging, seabed mining, aquaculture, or other marine and coastal land use changes.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to describe the extent of marine and coastal habitat loss resulting from financed activities during the reporting period. 

It captures the total surface area (in hectares) of marine ecosystems such as coral reefs, seagrass meadows, mangroves, saltmarshes, and other marine or intertidal habitats that have been negatively impacted, degraded, or permanently destroyed as a consequence of the financed activity. This includes both direct loss (e.g., from dredging, coastal construction, or seabed mining) and unrestored damage, meaning areas that remain ecologically impaired and have not been rehabilitated or restored. 

Losses should be reported even if restoration or mitigation efforts are planned but not yet implemented, and should include any areas that have been rendered ecologically unsuitable for the original habitat function or species use. 

Unit of measurement: Hectares.
Citation: IRIS, 2025. Loss of Marine Habitat (PI3227). v5.3b.

Definition: The total volume of plastic waste physically removed or diverted from natural environments, such as aquatic, marine, terrestrial, or urban ecosystems, through clean-up activities, waste interception infrastructure, or other interventions. This includes macroplastics and microplastics collected before entering or while present in these environments.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to measure the effectiveness of plastic waste removal efforts in reducing pollution and environmental harm across various ecosystems, including marine, freshwater, coastal, urban, and terrestrial settings. 

Unit of measurement: Kilograms (kg) or Metric Tons (tonnes). 

This metric is aligned with Global Reporting Initiatives Standards GRI 306 Waste: 2020
Citation: IRIS, 2025. Volume of Plastic Removed (PI3664). v5.3b.

Definition: The annual percentage change in the population size of a target species within a defined area, compared to a scientifically established baseline.
Footnote: Organizations should footnote all assumptions used.
Usage Guidance:
This metric is intended to assess the effectiveness of conservation and restoration interventions by tracking changes in the population of target species over time. 

SPRR=(Current Year Population−Baseline Population)/Baseline Population ×100 

This metric helps understand whether conservation or restoration efforts are leading to tangible improvements in species populations. It provides a standardized way to assess the effectiveness of conservation interventions aimed at restoring endangered or declining species.
